newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan politics seen casting shadow over stocks.
newsitem.headline: Japan politics seen casting shadow over stocks.

text.p: Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's new government looks set to weigh on the Tokyo stock market as it is considered unlikely to deliver the bold reforms that the economy needs, analysts say.

Hashimoto's choice of party elders for his cabinet team hardly inspires confidence in the likelihood of change, and the government's minority status means it could struggle to push through reforms to stimulate the economy, they say.
This is likely to act as a drag on stock prices.
"I cannot see any aggressiveness or leadership in the new line-up. I feel as if time has turned back to before 1993," said Shigenori Okazaki, a political analyst at SBC Warburg.

Hashimoto, who failed to cobble together a new coalition after his Liberal Democratic Party failed to win a majority in last month's elections, had to form a minority government on Thursday consisting entirely of LDP members.
It was the first all-LDP government since the party lost its post-war monopoly on power three years ago.

But the new cabinet, consisting of LDP old guard, is unlikely to come up with policies providing fresh buying incentives for the stock market, where participants are eagerly awaiting any drastic steps to help strengthen the country's nascent recovery, analysts said.
"Buying on the U.S. election is over, and the Japanese new cabinet will not become a buying factor," said Tetsuya Ishijima, chief strategist at Okasan Securities Co Ltd.
He said a lack of fresh faces in the ministers of finance, construction, transport and foreign affairs -- all of which affect financial markets -- could discourage the market.

Shinichi Ichikawa, strategist at Credit Lyonnais Securities, said foreign investors have been keeping a selling stance for the past half-year and will continue to do so, which is likely to put a damper on the market.
But there will be no particular sell-off by foreign investors either, as they had few hopes for the new government in the first place.
"The LDP remaining in power means there will be no drastic change. Many people think that whoever takes initiative, it would not make much difference," he said.

Ichikawa said the sharp rally which stocks enjoy periodically will keep bears from selling off, while the market will lack fresh factors to buy on. He expects the Nikkei average to be stuck between 19,000 and 21,500 until the end of the year.

On Thursday, the key 225-share Nikkei average slipped around one percent but the index bounced back sharply on Friday, rising just over than two percent, or 429.93 points, to 21,201.04 on technical buying.
Some foreign brokerages, meanwhile, saw the political developments in a relatively positive way.
"We think it's generally positive," said Tim Hayashida, strategist at Merrill Lynch Japan Inc.

"Regardless of who gains control of the Diet (parliament), that issue (administrative reforms) will remain and that ruling party will have to address the issue. In such a scenario, you have to wonder who would be in the best situation to act. At this point, it's the LDP," Hayashida said.
